newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somali gunmen free American aid worker.
newsitem.headline: Somali gunmen free American aid worker.

text.p: Gunmen released an American working for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) on Wednesday, a day after kidnapping him, aid and embassy officials said.
Aid officials said Daniel Suther, seized by at least eight gunmen in north Mogadishu, was freed in the town of Giohar, 70 km (40 miles) north of the capital.

A U.S. embassy spokesman in Nairobi said Suther was handed over to the aid agency Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors Without Borders) in Giohar. But an MSF-Spain official said that he had not been specifically passed on to its officials.
Aid workers said Suther was being driven to north Mogadishu and would fly out of Somalia on a U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) plane to the Kenyan capital Nairobi later on Wednesday.

On Tuesday, the gunmen disarmed Suther's two Somali guards and drove off with him and his Somali driver in a four-wheel-drive vehicle towards the coastal town of Uarsciek, 50 km (30 miles) northeast of the capital, security sources said.

They said Ali Mahdi Mohamed, whose Abgal clan alliance controls north Mogadishu, ordered an Islamic court to seize the kidnappers and also sent two "technicals" -- four-wheel-drive battlewagons -- to Uarsciek to recover the American.
Suther was taken shortly after meeting Ali Mahdi, they said.
In Washington, USAID spokeswoman Ann Kittlaus said on Tuesday that Suther was on contract to USAID and was a member of a three-person team sent to check on the food situation in north Mogadishu.
She said the other two members of the team were released and to USAID's knowledge everyone was safe including Suther.
Aid officials declined to comment on rumours that the American was seized from a WFP vehicle in a case of mistaken identity by gunmen who argued they were owed money by the U.N. agency.

Kidnappings and extortion, especially involving staff of foreign aid agencies, are common in Mogadishu, where weapons are easily available and unemployment is extremely high since the departure of the U.N. peacekeeping operation in March 1995.
International aid agencies pulled all foreign staff out of southern Mogadishu, controlled by forces loyal to faction leader Hussein Aideed, earlier this year, but kept some staff in north Mogadishu.
The northern part of the city was widely considered far less dangerous than the south for foreigners under the control of Ali Mahdi's forces and gunmen who enforce Islamic sharia law.

Islamic courts have been increasing their scope in recent months and earlier this month ordered that foreign aid workers and journalists in north Mogadishu could not be escorted by their own armed guards as the sector of the capital was safe.
Ali Mahdi supported U.S. military intervention in Somalia in December 1992 in Operation Restore Hope to help end famine and the subsequent U.N. peacekeeping operation in 1993 and 1994.

Somali gunmen have abducted more than 20 aid workers in the last three years in disputes over money. All were freed unharmed after negotiations but several foreigners were killed in other incidents. Somalia has had no central government or authority since the fall of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991.

The south Mogadishu-based faction led by Hussein Aideed said last Friday it would free within days a 25-year-old Australian pilot jailed for 25 years for making a forced landing in western Somalia in May.
